en: By whom impelled does the mind fly forth when sent?
By whom joined does the first breath proceed?
By whom impelled do they utter this speech? And which god joins together the eye and the ear? 1.1.
That which is the hearing of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speech of speech, and indeed the breath of the breath,
and the sight of the eye— having transcended these, the wise [attain liberation].
Having departed from this world, they become immortal. || 1.2 ||
Neither the eye goes there, nor speech, nor the mind; we do not know, nor do we understand how one might instruct this. 1.3.
"That is indeed other than the known, and moreover, it is above the unknown"—thus have we heard from those of old who explained it to us. 1.4.
That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed—that alone know thou to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here. 1.5.
That which the mind does not conceive, that by which they say the mind is conceived—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship. 1.6.
That which one does not see with the eye, that by which the eyes themselves are seen—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship. 1.7
That which one does not hear with the ear, by which this very ear is heard—that alone you should know as Brahman, and not that which people here worship as an object. 1.8.
That by which one breathes through the vital breath, that by which the vital breath is led forth—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship. 1.9
Thus ends the first section.
"I do not think that one knows well; nor does one not know. And yet, one knows. He who knows that we do not know it—he knows it; and he also knows that we do not know it. (2.2)
That which is not thought is thought by him; he who thinks it does not know it.
It is unknown to those who understand, and known to those who do not understand. 2.3.
That which is known through awakening is considered [the truth], for one finds immortality therein;
through the Self one finds vigor, and through knowledge one finds immortality. 2.4.
If one has known [the Self] here, then there is truth; if one has not known it here, there is great ruin.
Having searched among all beings, the wise [attain it].
Having departed from this world, they become immortal. || 2.6 ||
Thus ends the second section.
Brahman indeed conquered for the gods. In that victory of Brahman, the gods exulted. They thought, "This victory is ours alone; this greatness is ours alone. (3.1)
He indeed perceived them; he appeared before them. They did not recognize him, wondering, "What is this spirit?
They said to Agni: "O Jātavedas, find out what this spirit is. "So be it," he replied. 3.3.
He ran toward him. He addressed him, saying, "Who are you? He replied, "I am indeed Agni; I am indeed Jātavedas. (3.4)
"What power do you possess? [He replied: "I could burn all this that exists upon the earth. (3.5)

He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Burn this! It rushed toward it with all its speed, but it was unable to burn it. Thereupon it turned back from that very spot, saying, "I was not able to discern what this yakṣa is. (3.6)
Then they said to Vāyu, "Vāyu, find out what this Yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied. 3.7.
He ran toward him. He said to him, "Who are you? "I am indeed Vāyu," he replied; "I am Mātariśvan," he said. 3.8.
"What power do you possess? [He replied: "I could take up all this that is upon the earth. (3.9)

He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Take this. He rushed toward it with all his speed, but he was not able to take it. He turned back from that very spot, saying, "I was not able to discern what this yakṣa is. 3.10.
Then they said to Indra, "O Maghavan, find out what this yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied. He ran toward it, but it vanished from him. 3.11.
In that very space, he beheld a woman approaching, most radiant—Umā, the daughter of Himavat. He said to her, "What is this spirit? (3.12)
Thus ends the third section.
"It is Brahman," he said, "for it is in the victory of Brahman that you rejoice. Thereupon, he indeed understood: "It is Brahman. 4.1.1.
Therefore, these gods—namely Agni, Vāyu, and Indra—are, as it were, superior to the other gods; for they touched this [Brahman] most closely, and they were the first to recognize it as Brahman. 4.2.
Therefore, indeed, Indra surpasses the other gods; for he touched this most closely, and he was the first to know it as Brahman. 4.3.
This is its instruction: "As when lightning flashes, *ā3*—as when one closes one's eyes, *ā3*. This is with respect to the divine realm. 4.3.
Now, with reference to the self: that which is this mind, which, as it were, moves about, and by means of which one repeatedly recollects this—this is volition (saṅkalpa). 4.5.
Therefore, that [Self] is named "The Forest" (Tadvana). It should be meditated upon as "The Forest. He who knows this thus—indeed, all beings desire him. 4.6.
"Sir, tell me the Upanishad. "The Upanishad has been told to you. We have indeed told you the Upanishad concerning Brahman. 4.7.
For her, austerity, self-restraint, and ritual action are the foundation; the Vedas are all her limbs; and truth is her abode. 4.8.
Or whoever knows this thus, having struck away evil, becomes established in the infinite, unconquerable heavenly world; he becomes established. 4.9.
Thus ends the fourth section.
Thus ends the Kenopaniṣad.
